exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Derivative Using Multiple Instances of the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

\[ y = \sqrt{u}, \qquad u = \csc{v}, \qquad v = 5x + 2. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d v} = -\csc{v}\cot{v},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm d x} = 5. \]

Applying the chain rule twice, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d v}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} \cdot (-\csc v \cot v) \cdot 5\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{\csc(5x + 2)}} \cdot (-\csc(5x + 2) \cot(5x + 2)) \cdot 5\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{5}{2} \cot(5x + 2)\sqrt{\csc(5x + 2)}. \end{align*}

Now we compute $y'(0){:}$ \begin{align*} y'(0) &= -\dfrac{5}{2} \cot(5(0) + 2)\sqrt{\csc(5(0) + 2)}\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{5}{2} \cot(2)}\sqrt{\csc(2)}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Derivative Using Multiple Instances of the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
First, we express $f$ as the composite function

\[ f = \ln{u}, \qquad u = 2\sin{v}, \qquad v = e^x. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = \dfrac{1}{u},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d v} = 2\cos{v},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm d x} = e^x. \]

Applying now the chain rule twice, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d v}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{u} \cdot (2\cos{v}) \cdot e^x\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2\sin e^x} \cdot (2\cos(e^x)) \cdot e^x\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2e^x\cos(e^x)}{2\sin (e^x)} \\[5pt] &= e^x\dfrac{\cos (e^x)}{\sin (e^x)} \\[5pt] &=e^x\cot (e^x) \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules

question.explanation:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x}$ at that point.

This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x) = x^4$ and $v(x) = \csc(3x-1).$ Then

\[ u'(x) = 4x^3, \qquad v'(x) = -3\csc(3x-1)\cot(3x-1). \]

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

\[ \eqalign{ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} & = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x) \\[5pt] & = (4x^3)\left( \csc(3x-1) \right) + (x^4)\left( -3\csc(3x-1)\cot(3x-1) \right)\\[5pt] & = 4x^3\csc(3x-1) - 3x^4\csc(3x-1)\cot(3x-1) \\[5pt] & = x^3\csc(3x-1) \left( 4 - 3x\cot(3x-1) \right). } \]

Therefore, the slope at $x=1$ is

\begin{align} \left.\left(\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x}\right)\right|_{x=1} & = (1)^3\csc(3(1)-1) \left( 4 - 3(1)\cot(3(1)-1) \right) \\[5pt] & = \csc2 \left( 4 - 3\cot2 \right) . \end{align}

example.title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules

question.explanation:
This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x) = 2x^4$ and $v(x) = (5x+3)^2.$ Then

\[ u'(x) = 8x^3, \qquad v'(x) = 10(5x+3). \]

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

\[ \eqalign{ \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} & = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x) \\[5pt] & = (8x^3)(5x+3)^2 + (2x^4)\left(10(5x+3) \right)\\[5pt] & = 8x^3(5x+3)^2 + 20x^4(5x+3) \\[5pt] & = [8(5x+3)+20x]x^3(5x+3) \\[5pt] & = [60x+24]x^3(5x+3) \\[5pt] & = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{12x^3}(5x+2)(5x+3). } \]

question.explanation:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} $ at that point.

This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x) = x^2$ and $v(x) = \sin^3x.$ Then

\[ u'(x) = 2x, \qquad v'(x) = 3\sin^2x \cos x. \]

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

\[ \eqalign{ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} & = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x) \\[3pt] & = (2x)\left( \sin^3x \right) + (x^2)\left( 3\sin^2x \cos x \right)\\[3pt] & = 2x\sin^3x + 3x^2\sin^2x \cos x . } \]

Therefore, the slope at $x=0$ is

\begin{align} \left.\left(\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x}\right)\right|_{x=0} & = 2\cdot 0 \cdot \sin^3 (0) + 3\cdot 0^2 \cdot \sin^2 (0) \cos (0)\\ & =0. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules

question.explanation:
This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x) = x$ and $v(x) = \ln (x+1).$ Then

\[ u'(x) = 1, \qquad v'(x) = \dfrac{1}{x+1}. \]

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

\[ \eqalign{ \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} & = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x) \\[5pt] & = (1)(\ln (x+1)) + (x)\left( \dfrac{1}{x+1} \right)\\[5pt] & = \ln (x+1) + \dfrac{x}{x+1}. } \]

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules

question.explanation:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x) = \sqrt{\ln x}$ and the denominator $v(x) = 2x.$

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

\[ u'(x) = \dfrac{1}{2x\sqrt{\ln x}}, \qquad v'(x) = 2. \]

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ y' = \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &= \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\left(\dfrac{1}{2x\sqrt{\ln x}}\right)(2x) - (\sqrt{\ln x})(2)}{(2x)^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\ln x}} - 2\sqrt{\ln x}}{4x^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {1 - 2\ln x}{4x^2\sqrt{\ln x}} . } \end{eqnarray}

example.title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules

question.explanation:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x) = \ln (x^3)$ and the denominator $v(x) = x^3 +2.$

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

\[ u'(x) = \dfrac{3}{x}, \qquad v'(x) = 3x^2. \]

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ y'=\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &= \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\left(\dfrac{3}{x}\right)(x^3 +2) - \left(\ln (x^3)\right) (3x^2)}{(x^3+2)^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {3(x^3 +2) - 3x^3\ln (x^3)}{x(x^3+2)^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {3x^3 - 3x^3\ln (x^3)+6}{x(x^3+2)^2} . } \end{eqnarray}
